resources.title: Periodic table
resources.summary: An interactive periodic table, following the one AQA prints in every Chemistry exam. Press any element for its atomic number, relative atomic mass and what those tell you; press a family to pick it out.
resources.statusNote: AQA prints the table in every paper. It gives each element's symbol, name, atomic number and relative atomic mass, rounded to whole numbers except copper (63.5) and chlorine (35.5). It does **not** give ion charges or the reactivity series: those you learn.

sources.name: AQA GCSE Chemistry specification (8462)
sources.where: Section 9, Appendix A (an older printing: elements 113, 115, 117 and 118 carry temporary names)

applications.title: Predicting before testing
applications.body: Mendeleev left gaps in his table for elements nobody had found, and predicted their properties from their neighbours. Gallium and germanium were found later and matched.

applications.title: Choosing materials
applications.body: Engineers who need a light, strong metal look along Groups 2 and 3 and the lighter transition metals, which is why aircraft use aluminium and titanium alloys.

applications.title: Working out a formula
applications.body: Sodium is in Group 1 and forms Na⁺; chlorine in Group 7 forms Cl⁻. The group alone tells you that table salt is NaCl.

blocks.alt: An interactive periodic table of the 90 elements on the AQA insert, coloured by family, with a panel that shows the pressed element's symbol, name, atomic number, relative atomic mass and family

blocks.body:
**Reading a cell.** The number on top is the relative atomic mass: the average mass of the element's atoms. The number at the bottom is the atomic number: the number of protons, which is also the number of electrons in the atom.

**Finding the neutrons.** For the first 20 elements, take the atomic number from the mass: sodium, $23 - 11 = 12$ neutrons. Chlorine is the exception. Its mass, 35.5, is an average of two kinds of chlorine atom, so it is not a whole number. An exam question on neutrons gives you the mass number of the atom it means.

**Reading the layout.** A **row** is a period: every element in it has the same number of electron shells. A **column** is a group: the same number of electrons in the outer shell, which is why the elements in it react alike. The group number is that number of electrons. Group 0 is the exception: its atoms have eight, and helium has two. The ten columns in the middle with no number are the transition metals. Hydrogen stands on its own, in no group.

resources.title: Common ions
resources.summary: The charges on the ions you meet in the course, positive and negative, including the ions made of more than one atom, and how to use them to write the formula of a compound.

applications.title: Reading a water bottle label
applications.body: The minerals listed on bottled water, calcium Ca²⁺, magnesium Mg²⁺, sodium Na⁺, chloride Cl⁻ and sulfate SO₄²⁻, are these ions, measured in milligrams per litre.

applications.title: Fertilisers
applications.body: A bag of fertiliser lists ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃: one ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, for every nitrate, NO₃⁻, because their charges cancel one for one.

blocks.title: Positive ions
rows: hydrogen $\text{H}^{+}$, lithium $\text{Li}^{+}$, sodium $\text{Na}^{+}$, potassium $\text{K}^{+}$, silver $\text{Ag}^{+}$, ammonium $\text{NH}_4^{+}$
magnesium $\text{Mg}^{2+}$, calcium $\text{Ca}^{2+}$, barium $\text{Ba}^{2+}$, copper(II) $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, iron(II) $\text{Fe}^{2+}$, zinc $\text{Zn}^{2+}$
blocks.note: Metals form positive ions. So do hydrogen and ammonium, which are not metals. A Roman numeral in a name gives the charge where a metal can have more than one: iron(II) is $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ and iron(III) is $\text{Fe}^{3+}$.

blocks.title: Negative ions
blocks.note: Non-metals form negative ions. Hydroxide, nitrate, sulfate and carbonate are each made of more than one atom, and the charge belongs to the whole group.

blocks.body:
**What an ion is.** An atom, or a group of atoms, with a charge, because it has lost or gained electrons. Losing electrons leaves a positive ion. Gaining them makes a negative ion.

**From the group.** Atoms in Group 1 lose one electron, so they form $1+$ ions. Group 2 lose two: $2+$. Group 7 gain one: $1-$. Group 6 gain two: $2-$. The other charges in the tables cannot be read from the group in this way. Learn them: silver $1+$, zinc $2+$, aluminium $3+$, copper(II), iron(II), iron(III), and the ions made of more than one atom.

**Writing a formula.** The charges must add up to zero. Write the two ions, then find how many of each make the charges cancel.

- **Sodium chloride.** $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$: $+1$ and $-1$ cancel one for one, so $\text{NaCl}$.
- **Magnesium chloride.** $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$: one magnesium ion gives $+2$, so it needs two chloride ions, $-2$. The formula is $\text{MgCl}_2$.
- **Calcium hydroxide.** $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{OH}^{-}$: one calcium ion needs two hydroxide ions. Hydroxide is made of two atoms, so it goes in a bracket: $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$.
- **Aluminium sulfate.** $\text{Al}^{3+}$ and $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$: two aluminium ions give $+6$ and three sulfate ions give $-6$, so $\text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3$.

A bracket goes round an ion made of more than one atom, and only when the formula needs more than one of that ion. The charges are not written in the finished formula.

resources.title: Reactivity series
resources.summary: The metals the specification names, most reactive first, with carbon and hydrogen placed among them, how each reacts with water and dilute acid at room temperature, and what the order decides.

blocks.title: Most reactive at the top
rows: reacts violently: fizzes, melts, and the hydrogen burns lilac
reacts vigorously: fizzes and melts into a ball that skims about
barely: a few bubbles over days
*not a metal: placed here as a marker*
*not a metal: see the note for what the marker shows*
*not a metal: placed here as a marker*
*not a metal: see the note for what the marker shows*
blocks.note: Carbon and hydrogen are non-metals. They are in the list as markers. A metal below carbon can be extracted from its oxide by heating with carbon. A metal below hydrogen does not react with dilute acid. All reactions are at room temperature: the specification does not include reactions with steam. A metal that reacts gives off hydrogen, and the faster the fizzing, the more reactive the metal.

blocks.body:
**What the order decides.**

- **Displacement.** A more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive one in a compound. To predict it, find both metals in the list. If the metal you add is higher than the metal in the compound, it displaces it. Zinc is above copper, so zinc in copper sulfate solution gives zinc sulfate and a coating of copper. Copper is below zinc, so copper in zinc sulfate solution does nothing.
- **Extraction.** Metals below carbon, such as zinc, iron and copper, can be extracted by heating their oxides with carbon. The carbon takes the oxygen. Metals above carbon, such as sodium and aluminium, are too reactive for that. They are extracted by electrolysis: the compound is melted and split with an electric current. Aluminium is not one of the eight metals to learn in order. It sits between magnesium and carbon.
- **Why the order.** A reactive metal loses its outer electrons easily to form a positive ion. Going up the series, that happens more readily.

**A mnemonic.** *Please Send Lions, Cats, Monkeys, Cute Zebras Into Hot Countries*: potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, carbon, zinc, iron, hydrogen, copper. Three words start with C. They stand for calcium, carbon and copper, in that order.

applications.title: Why gold is found as gold
applications.body: Gold is so unreactive that it sits below copper and is found in the ground as the metal itself, while sodium, near the top, is only ever found in compounds.

applications.title: Protecting a ship
applications.body: Blocks of zinc bolted to a steel hull corrode instead of the iron in the steel, because zinc is more reactive. This is called sacrificial protection. Galvanising, which coats iron with zinc, works the same way.

resources.title: Chemical tests
resources.summary: The tests for gases and for ions that the specification lists, each with the result it gives: the four gases, flame colours, the metal hydroxide precipitates, and the tests for carbonates, halides and sulfates.

blocks.title: Gases
rows: a burning splint at the mouth of the tube
a glowing splint in the tube
blocks.note: Limewater is a solution of calcium hydroxide in water.

blocks.title: Flame tests (Chemistry only)
blocks.note: Dip a clean wire loop in the sample and hold it in a blue Bunsen flame. In a mixture, one colour can hide another: the strong yellow of sodium masks the rest.

blocks.title: Add sodium hydroxide solution (Chemistry only)
blocks.note: A precipitate is a solid that forms when two solutions are mixed. It turns the liquid cloudy. Add a few drops of sodium hydroxide solution, then keep adding: that is adding it in excess. Only aluminium hydroxide dissolves in excess, which tells it apart from calcium and magnesium. To tell calcium from magnesium, use a flame test: calcium gives orange-red.

blocks.title: Negative ions (Chemistry only)
rows: add dilute acid, bubble the gas through limewater
add dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution
add dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution
add dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution
add dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride solution

blocks.body: **Putting tests together.** An unknown salt gives a lilac flame, so it contains potassium ions, $\text{K}^{+}$. With dilute hydrochloric acid and barium chloride solution it gives a white precipitate, so it contains sulfate ions, $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$. The salt is potassium sulfate, $\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4$.

applications.title: Fireworks
applications.body: A firework's colours are flame colours. Strontium or lithium salts burn red, calcium salts orange and sodium salts yellow. Makers mix salts to get the colours between.

applications.title: Testing tap water
applications.body: Water companies check tap water for ions such as chloride and sulfate. They use instruments, which are faster and more accurate than test-tube tests and can find much smaller amounts.

resources.title: pH scale and indicators
resources.summary: The pH scale from 0 to 14 in the colours universal indicator turns, with everyday substances placed on it, how pH is measured and, for Higher tier, what a change of one pH unit means.

visual.alt: The pH scale from 0 to 14 as a bar coloured red through orange, yellow, green, blue and purple, with stomach acid, lemon juice, vinegar, pure water, baking soda solution, soap and oven cleaner listed with their pH values and colours

blocks.body:
**Below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline.** Acids release hydrogen ions, $\text{H}^{+}$, in water. Alkalis release hydroxide ions, $\text{OH}^{-}$. A base is a substance that neutralises an acid, and an alkali is a base that dissolves in water. In neutralisation the two ions make water: $\text{H}^{+}\text{(aq)} + \text{OH}^{-}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$.

**Measuring pH.** Universal indicator is a mixture of dyes. Add a few drops, or dip indicator paper, and match the colour to the chart. It gives an approximate pH. A pH probe gives a reading on a meter instead.

**Higher tier.** Each fall of one pH unit means ten times the concentration of hydrogen ions. A solution of pH 2 has ten times the hydrogen ion concentration of one at pH 3, and a hundred times that of one at pH 4.

applications.title: Swimming pools
applications.body: Pool water is kept at about pH 7.2 to 7.6. Any lower and it stings the eyes; any higher and the chlorine that keeps it clean stops working well.

applications.title: Soil and gardening
applications.body: Farmers test soil pH and spread lime, a base, on acidic fields, because most crops grow best near neutral.

applications.title: Indigestion tablets
applications.body: They contain a base such as calcium carbonate that neutralises excess stomach acid, raising its pH.

resources.title: Structures and bonding
resources.summary: The four kinds of structure side by side: ionic, simple molecular, giant covalent and metallic, each drawn, with what holds it together and the properties that follow.

blocks.title: Structure decides properties
rows: strong attraction between oppositely charged ions, in every direction
when melted or dissolved, as the ions can move
strong covalent bonds inside each molecule; weak forces between molecules
no: the molecules have no overall charge
no, except graphite, which has delocalised electrons
positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons
yes, as the delocalised electrons move
blocks.note: Giant means the pattern repeats through the whole piece, with no separate molecules. A lattice is a regular, repeating arrangement. Delocalised electrons are outer electrons that are free to move through the whole structure, so they can carry charge.

blocks.body: **Working backwards.** A white solid melts at 801 °C. It does not conduct electricity as a solid, but it does when melted. The high melting point rules out simple molecular. Conducting only when melted means charged particles that are fixed in the solid and free in the liquid: ions. The structure is ionic. This one is sodium chloride.

visual.alt: A giant ionic lattice: alternating positive and negative ions in a regular grid

blocks.caption: **Ionic.** A giant lattice of positive and negative ions.

visual.alt: Simple molecules: pairs of atoms strongly bonded, scattered with weak forces between the molecules

blocks.caption: **Simple molecular.** Small molecules, drawn here as pairs of atoms such as oxygen. The bonds inside each molecule are strong. The forces between molecules are weak, so little energy separates them.

visual.alt: A giant covalent lattice such as diamond: every atom bonded to its neighbours

blocks.caption: **Giant covalent: diamond.** In diamond every carbon atom is bonded to four others, in three dimensions. This flat sketch shows a small piece, so the atoms at its edges are drawn with fewer bonds. In the real structure the pattern carries on.

visual.alt: Graphite: two layers of hexagons with weak forces between the layers

blocks.caption: **Giant covalent: graphite.** Layers of joined hexagons. Each carbon is bonded to three others in its layer, and one electron from each carbon is delocalised. There are no covalent bonds between the layers.

visual.alt: Metallic structure: rows of positive ions with delocalised electrons between them

blocks.caption: **Metallic.** Positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons.

applications.title: Pencils
applications.body: A pencil writes because graphite's layers slide off onto the paper: the forces between layers are weak, though every layer is held together by strong covalent bonds.

applications.title: Gritting roads
applications.body: Salt is ionic, so it does not melt in winter; it dissolves in the water on the road instead, and the salty solution freezes at a lower temperature.

resources.title: Homologous series
resources.summary: The four families of organic compounds in the course: alkanes, alkenes, alcohols and carboxylic acids, with their functional groups and first four members, and two of each family drawn in full.

blocks.body:
**What a homologous series is.** A family of compounds that share a functional group and a general formula. Each member has one more carbon atom than the one before. The functional group is the part of the molecule that reacts, so members of a family react in the same way.

**Using a general formula.** Put the number of carbons in place of $n$. Propane has three carbons, so the alkane formula $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n+2}$ gives $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8$. Propene also has three, so the alkene formula $\text{C}_n\text{H}_{2n}$ gives $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6$.

blocks.title: Four families
rows: none: every bond is a single bond
methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic and butanoic acid
blocks.note: The name tells you the carbons: *meth-* one, *eth-* two, *prop-* three, *but-* four, *pent-* five. The ending tells you the family: *-ane*, *-ene*, *-ol*, *-oic acid*. The alkenes start at ethene, because a double bond between carbons needs two carbons.

visual.alt: The displayed formulae of ethane and ethene side by side, showing that ethene has a double bond between its two carbons and two fewer hydrogen atoms

props.title: Two fewer hydrogens, and a second bond in their place

blocks.caption: **Alkane and alkene.** Ethane is saturated: every bond is single, so it holds as many hydrogens as it can. Ethene is unsaturated: its double bond takes the place of two hydrogens.

visual.alt: The displayed formulae of methanol and ethanol, each showing the oxygen hydrogen group drawn as an O joined to an H at the end of the carbon chain

props.title: Every bond drawn, including the O-H

blocks.caption: **Alcohols.** The –OH group on the end carbon.

visual.alt: The displayed formulae of methanoic acid and ethanoic acid, each showing the carboxyl group with one oxygen double bonded to the carbon and the other joined to a hydrogen

props.title: One carbon, two oxygens: the -COOH group

blocks.caption: **Carboxylic acids.** The –COOH group: one oxygen double bonded, one with a hydrogen.

applications.title: Fuels
applications.body: Methane is natural gas. Propane and butane fill camping gas canisters. Petrol is a mixture of larger hydrocarbons, mostly alkanes. With plenty of air, all of them burn to carbon dioxide and water.

applications.title: Vinegar and hand gel
applications.body: Vinegar is a dilute solution of ethanoic acid, a carboxylic acid; hand sanitiser is mostly ethanol, an alcohol.

resources.title: Required practicals
resources.summary: The eight required practicals in AQA Chemistry: what each investigates and what you measure. Two, titration and identifying ions, are Chemistry only.

blocks.title: The eight required practicals
rows: add an insoluble oxide or carbonate to hot dilute acid until no more reacts, filter off what is left, warm the solution until crystals start to form, then leave it to crystallise
a pure, dry sample of the salt
measure 25 cm³ of alkali into a flask with a pipette, add indicator, then run in acid from a burette until the colour changes
the reacting volumes; at Higher tier, a concentration in mol/dm³ and g/dm³
pass an electric current through salt solutions, using electrodes that do not react, such as carbon rods
react solutions such as acid and metal, or acid and alkali
the temperature change, and what affects it
run a reaction at different concentrations, by two methods
the volume of gas given off over time, and the time for a solution to turn cloudy
the $R_f$ value of each spot: the distance the spot moved divided by the distance the solvent moved
run the flame, hydroxide, carbonate, halide and sulfate tests
which ions an unknown compound holds
test samples from different sources, and distil one
the pH and dissolved solids, and pure water
blocks.note: AQA says questions drawing on the practicals count for at least 15% of the marks. Know the method, the variables and the hazards of each. An $R_f$ example: a spot moves 3.0 cm while the solvent moves 6.0 cm, so $R_f = 3.0 \div 6.0 = 0.50$.

applications.title: Forensic science
applications.body: Chromatography separates the inks in a forged document or the dyes in a fibre, and $R_f$ values identify them against known samples.

applications.title: Drinking water
applications.body: Water companies test pH and dissolved solids, as you do in practical 8. In the UK they make water safe by filtering and sterilising it. Where fresh water is short, sea water is distilled or forced through membranes, which takes a lot of energy.
